subject: ela
intro: Skilled speakers do not just sound formal. They weigh what each audience and purpose actually calls for, then adjust tone and word choice to fit. In these problems you will compare versions of a statement, judge speech for two different audiences, and decide which adaptation truly fits, remembering that the most formal option is not always the best one and that meaning must never change.

items.prompt: Maya will give the same news in two settings. First she reports a science fair result to the school board, then she tells her best friend about it at lunch. To the board she says, 'Our project demonstrated that recycled paper absorbs more water than new paper.' To her friend she says, 'Okay so basically the recycled stuff soaked up way more water, it was wild.' A classmate argues that Maya was wrong to change her words and should have used the board version with everyone. Evaluate this claim and explain what Maya actually did well.
items.answer: The classmate is wrong. Maya correctly adapted her speech to two different contexts. The formal board version fits a serious, official audience, while the casual friend version fits a relaxed, personal conversation, and both report the same finding.

steps: Identify the two contexts: a school board (formal, official, public) and a best friend at lunch (informal, personal, relaxed).
Check that both statements carry the same idea: recycled paper absorbed more water than new paper. They do, so meaning was preserved.
Recognize that formal is not automatically better. Speaking to a friend the way she speaks to the board would sound stiff and out of place.
Conclude the classmate is wrong: Maya matched tone and word choice to each audience and purpose, which is exactly the skill of adapting speech to context.

items.prompt: Devon is presenting his community garden proposal to the city council. He wants the council to take him seriously and fund the project. He is choosing between two openings. Version 1: 'Honestly, gardens are super cool and our neighborhood could totally use one, no cap.' Version 2: 'A community garden would provide fresh produce and a shared space for our neighborhood, and I am asking the council to support it.' Which version best fits this context, and why is the other a poor choice?
items.answer: Version 2 is the better choice. It uses formal, respectful language suited to an official council request, while Version 1 relies on slang ('super cool,' 'totally,' 'no cap') that is too casual for a formal funding request.

steps: Identify the audience and purpose: a city council, with the goal of being taken seriously and securing funding. This is a formal context.
Examine Version 1 for register markers: 'honestly,' 'super cool,' 'totally,' and 'no cap' are slang and fillers that signal casual speech.
Examine Version 2: it states the benefit and the request in clear, formal English with no slang.
Conclude Version 2 best fits the formal context, while Version 1 is a poor choice because its casual register undercuts a serious request.

items.prompt: During a formal classroom presentation on water pollution, Priya says: 'Pollution from factories harms local rivers. The contaminated water then affects fish and the people who eat them. Anyway, long story short, it is kind of a big mess and we should probably do something.' Her teacher grades on appropriate formal speech. Identify the part of Priya's presentation that does not fit the formal context, and revise it to match while keeping her meaning.
items.answer: The mismatched part is 'Anyway, long story short, it is kind of a big mess and we should probably do something.' A formal revision could be: 'In short, this is a serious problem that requires action.'

steps: Note the context: a formal classroom presentation graded on formal speech.
Scan for casual markers: 'Anyway,' 'long story short,' 'kind of,' and 'probably' are conversational fillers and hedges that clash with the formal tone of the first two sentences.
Keep the underlying meaning: the situation is a serious problem and action is needed.
Revise to formal English without changing that meaning: 'In short, this is a serious problem that requires action.'

items.prompt: Jordan must explain the same safety rule to two audiences: a panel of teachers reviewing the lab and a group of younger students he is mentoring. To the teachers he says, 'Students must wear goggles at all times when chemicals are in use.' To the younger students he says, 'Hey everyone, make sure you keep your goggles on whenever we are working with chemicals, okay?' Evaluate whether Jordan adapted well, and justify your judgment.
items.answer: Jordan adapted well. The formal version fits an official teacher panel, and the warmer, friendlier version fits younger students he is mentoring, while both communicate the same rule that goggles must be worn around chemicals.

steps: Identify the two audiences and purposes: a teacher panel (formal review) and younger students (a mentoring, approachable setting).
Compare the statements: both require goggles whenever chemicals are in use, so the meaning is identical.
Judge the register for each: formal, precise wording suits the panel, while a friendlier, encouraging tone suits younger learners.
Conclude Jordan adapted well, because he matched tone to each listener without changing the safety message.

items.prompt: At a casual after-school club meeting where friends plan a fun movie night, Leo stands up and announces: 'I hereby propose that this assembly formally deliberate upon the selection of a cinematic feature for our forthcoming gathering.' The other members look confused. Explain why Leo's speech does not fit this context, even though it is very formal, and suggest a better statement.
items.answer: Leo's speech is too stiff and formal for a casual club planning a fun movie night. Overly formal language is a mismatch here. A better statement is: 'Let's vote on which movie to watch for movie night.'

steps: Identify the context: a casual, friendly after-school club planning a fun event. This calls for relaxed, conversational speech.
Recognize the key idea that formal is not always better. Leo's wording ('I hereby propose,' 'formally deliberate,' 'cinematic feature') is far too stiff for friends having fun.
Confirm the mismatch: the audience is confused because the formality does not fit the relaxed purpose.
Suggest speech that fits: 'Let's vote on which movie to watch for movie night,' which is clear and appropriately casual.

items.prompt: Aisha is interviewing for a volunteer position at the public library. The librarian asks why she wants the job. Aisha considers three answers. A) 'I love books and I think it would be a great way to help my community.' B) 'Books are awesome and honestly the library is kinda the best, so yeah.' C) 'I do really enjoy reading, but more than that I want to give back to my neighborhood.' Two of these fit a job interview. Identify the one that does NOT fit and explain why, then state which of the remaining two is strongest.
items.answer: Option B does not fit. It uses slang and fillers ('awesome,' 'kinda,' 'so yeah') that are too casual for a job interview. Of the remaining two, Option C is strongest because it gives a thoughtful, formal reason centered on service.

steps: Identify the context: a volunteer job interview, a semi-formal setting where polite, clear speech is expected.
Examine Option B: 'awesome,' 'kinda,' and 'so yeah' are casual markers that do not suit an interview, so it does not fit.
Compare the fitting options A and C: both are appropriately formal and sincere.
Judge C as strongest because it goes beyond liking books to a stronger motive, giving back to the neighborhood, which best answers why she wants the role.

items.prompt: Sam wrote a formal speech about a serious topic, the loss of local wildlife habitat. He believes that because the topic is so serious, his speech must already be formal enough. His draft reads: 'Losing habitat is a huge deal for animals. Tons of them are basically getting kicked out of their homes, and that is super not okay.' Explain the mistake in Sam's reasoning and revise his speech to truly match a formal context.
items.answer: Sam wrongly judges formality by how serious the topic is rather than by his word choice. His draft uses casual phrasing ('huge deal,' 'tons of,' 'basically,' 'kicked out,' 'super not okay'). A formal revision: 'The loss of habitat is a serious problem for animals. Many of them are being driven from their homes, which is unacceptable.'

steps: Name Sam's error: he assumes a serious topic makes speech formal, but formality comes from word choice and tone, not the subject.
Identify the casual markers in his draft: 'huge deal,' 'Tons of,' 'basically,' 'kicked out,' and 'super not okay.'
Keep the meaning: habitat loss seriously harms animals by forcing them from their homes, and it is wrong.
Revise to formal English: 'The loss of habitat is a serious problem for animals. Many of them are being driven from their homes, which is unacceptable.'

items.prompt: Nina is recording two messages about the same event, a class fundraiser. One is a public announcement read over the school intercom to the whole school, and one is a quick voice message to her teammate Carlos about meeting up early. Message for the intercom: 'The sixth grade fundraiser will be held Friday at noon in the gymnasium. All students are welcome.' Message for Carlos: 'Hey Carlos, can you get there a little early Friday so we can set up? Thanks.' A friend says both messages should sound exactly the same. Evaluate that advice and justify your answer.
items.answer: The advice is wrong. The two messages have different audiences and purposes, so they should not sound the same. The formal intercom announcement suits the whole school, while the casual message to Carlos suits a quick note to a teammate.

steps: Identify the two contexts: a school-wide intercom announcement (formal, public) and a personal message to a teammate (informal, one-on-one).
Recognize that the same speech does not fit every audience. Adapting tone to the listener is the goal.
Check each message fits its audience: the announcement is clear and formal, the note to Carlos is friendly and brief.
Conclude the friend's advice is wrong, because matching one fixed tone to both audiences would ignore who is listening and why.

items.prompt: Two students revise the casual statement 'We kinda figured the experiment was a flop' for a formal lab report presentation. Revision X: 'We concluded that the experiment was unsuccessful.' Revision Y: 'We were certain the experiment was a complete disaster that ruined everything.' Decide which revision is correct for a formal context and explain why the other revision is flawed.
items.answer: Revision X is correct. It states the same idea in formal English. Revision Y is flawed because, while it sounds dramatic, it changes the meaning by overstating from 'kinda figured' to 'were certain' and from 'a flop' to 'a complete disaster that ruined everything.'

steps: Restate the original meaning: the students roughly figured (were not certain) that the experiment did not work.
Evaluate Revision X: 'concluded' and 'unsuccessful' are formal, and the meaning still reflects a measured judgment that it failed.
Evaluate Revision Y: it changes 'kinda figured' to 'were certain' and exaggerates 'a flop' into 'a complete disaster that ruined everything,' altering the meaning.
Conclude Revision X is correct because a good formal revision adjusts register without changing what was said.

items.prompt: Carmen is the student speaker at a formal awards ceremony attended by parents, teachers, and the principal. Midway through her prepared remarks she says: 'And the science teachers? Total legends. They saved us when our projects were, like, falling apart.' Identify why this portion mismatches the ceremony, and revise it to fit while keeping the praise for the science teachers.
items.answer: The portion mismatches because 'Total legends,' 'like,' and 'falling apart' are casual slang and fillers unsuited to a formal ceremony. A revision: 'I am especially grateful to the science teachers, who supported us when our projects faced serious difficulties.'

steps: Set the context: a formal awards ceremony with parents, teachers, and the principal, which calls for dignified speech.
Spot the casual markers: 'Total legends,' the filler 'like,' and the loose phrase 'falling apart' clash with the formal occasion.
Preserve the meaning: she is praising and thanking the science teachers for helping when projects struggled.
Revise to formal English: 'I am especially grateful to the science teachers, who supported us when our projects faced serious difficulties.'

items.prompt: A debate coach gives feedback to two students who described the same proposal to a panel of judges. Student 1 said: 'Our plan will reduce waste because it sets clear recycling rules for every classroom.' Student 2 said: 'Our plan is, like, gonna cut down on garbage and stuff since classrooms would have to recycle and whatnot.' The coach must explain which delivery better fits a formal debate. Compare the two and justify which one the judges would find more appropriate.
items.answer: Student 1's delivery better fits a formal debate. It states the plan and its reason in clear, formal English. Student 2 uses slang and fillers ('like,' 'gonna,' 'and stuff,' 'and whatnot') that are too casual for judges in a formal debate.

steps: Identify the context: a formal debate judged by a panel, which expects precise, formal speech.
Confirm both students make the same point: the plan reduces waste through classroom recycling rules.
Compare register: Student 1 is clear and formal, while Student 2 is loaded with fillers ('like,' 'and stuff,' 'and whatnot') and casual contractions ('gonna').
Justify the choice: judges would find Student 1 more appropriate because the formal register matches the seriousness and purpose of the debate.

items.prompt: Tariq is texting a group chat of close friends to plan a casual bike ride this weekend. He writes: 'It would be most agreeable if the assembled parties could convene at the park at precisely ten o'clock for our recreational excursion.' His friends are baffled. A classmate insists the message is excellent because it is so polished and formal. Evaluate that opinion and explain what a well-adapted message would look like.
items.answer: The opinion is wrong. The message is too formal and stiff for a casual text to close friends, so its polish actually makes it a mismatch. A well-adapted message would be casual, such as: 'Hey, want to meet at the park around 10 for a bike ride this weekend?'

steps: Identify the context: a casual group text to close friends planning a fun bike ride, which calls for relaxed, friendly speech.
Recognize that formal is not always better. The stiff wording ('most agreeable,' 'assembled parties,' 'recreational excursion') does not fit a casual text.
Confirm the mismatch: the friends are baffled because the formality clashes with the relaxed purpose.
Describe a well-adapted message: a short, friendly text like 'Hey, want to meet at the park around 10 for a bike ride this weekend?'

items.prompt: Grace is preparing to present survey results to two audiences on the same day: first the school principal in a formal meeting, then her classmates during an informal study group. She drafts one line she plans to use word for word in both: 'Yo, the data shows most kids want longer lunch, which is honestly a slam dunk argument.' Explain why this single line cannot fit both audiences, and describe how she should adapt it for each.
items.answer: The line cannot fit both because it is casual ('Yo,' 'kids,' 'honestly,' 'slam dunk argument'), which is fine for the study group but too informal for a formal meeting with the principal. For the principal: 'The data show that most students want a longer lunch, which strongly supports the proposal.' For classmates the casual version is acceptable.

steps: Identify the two contexts: a formal meeting with the principal and an informal study group with classmates.
Examine the line's register: 'Yo,' 'kids,' 'honestly,' and 'slam dunk argument' are casual markers.
Explain the conflict: the same casual line fits the study group but is too informal for the principal, so one wording cannot serve both audiences.
Adapt for each: keep a casual tone for classmates, and for the principal use formal English such as 'The data show that most students want a longer lunch, which strongly supports the proposal.'

items.prompt: In a formal presentation to a panel of local business owners, Eli says: 'Our app is honestly a game changer and super easy, you will totally love it, trust me.' A teammate suggests this revision: 'Our app offers a significant improvement and is simple to use, and we believe you will find it valuable.' A second teammate argues the original is better because it sounds more excited and friendly. Evaluate both views and decide which version fits the panel.
items.answer: The revised version fits the panel. It states the same points in formal, professional English suited to business owners. The original uses slang and fillers ('honestly,' 'game changer,' 'super,' 'totally,' 'trust me') that are too casual, so the second teammate's view is mistaken.

steps: Identify the context: a formal presentation to local business owners, which calls for professional speech.
Examine the original: 'honestly,' 'game changer,' 'super,' 'totally,' and 'trust me' are casual and may sound unconvincing to a professional panel.
Examine the revision: it conveys the same claims (a big improvement, easy to use, valuable) in formal English.
Decide: the revised version fits the panel, and being excited or friendly does not outweigh the need for an appropriately formal register here, so the second teammate is mistaken.

items.prompt: A teacher asks the class to judge which speaker adapted best. Speaker A spoke to a panel of scientists and said, 'Our results were super cool and kinda surprising.' Speaker B spoke to a group of kindergarten students and said, 'The empirical findings exhibited a statistically notable deviation.' Speaker C spoke to the school board and said, 'Our results were significant and unexpected, and they support further study.' Evaluate all three and explain which speaker adapted speech to context best and why the other two did not.
items.answer: Speaker C adapted best, using clear formal language suited to the school board. Speaker A was too casual ('super cool,' 'kinda') for a panel of scientists, and Speaker B was far too technical and stiff for kindergarten students, so both mismatched their audiences.

steps: Evaluate Speaker A: a panel of scientists is a formal audience, but 'super cool' and 'kinda surprising' are casual, so the register is too low.
Evaluate Speaker B: kindergarten students need simple speech, but 'empirical findings' and 'statistically notable deviation' are far too technical and stiff, showing that formal is not always better.
Evaluate Speaker C: a school board is a formal audience, and the clear, formal wording fits the audience and purpose well.
Conclude Speaker C adapted best, because each of the others failed to match tone and word choice to the specific listener.
